title: Letter 43 — On Unseasonable Merriment
attribution_note: Letter 43 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: Merriment while the wrath of God is near

pairs.en: Word is heard that in certain cities the inhabitants, imitating those places where the wrath of God appeared through the pestilence and smote several thousands, gather together and make merry by turns — now at one man's house, now at another's. Whether this is done among you is unknown. Hearken, then, ye who so gather and make merry.

sections.heading: Wealth is a stewardship, not a possession

pairs.en: 1) If thou hadst given a man a hundred, or some other sum of money, and hadst charged him that he himself should be content therewith, and should supply the poor, and he either kept it all for himself, or squandered it only on his own whims — say, would it not be an offence and a grief both to thee and to the poor, whom he ought to supply with thy goods given him? Truly both to thee and to them it would be an injury!

God gives substance and riches to men for this end: that they themselves should be content with them in moderation, and should supply the poor therewith. But when men either keep them locked in their chests, or waste them on luxury and whims, they do a like offence — or even a far greater — to God, and an injury to the poor. For all rich men are stewards and overseers of God, and not owners.

God alone is the Owner and Lord of every good thing and of all riches; and to whomsoever He will, He gives them, and gives them for the common good. Thou callest thy steward to account for the money given him — where and upon what he has spent it; and the Lord likewise calleth thee to account for the riches given thee by Him, and for every rouble, upon what thou hast spent it, thou shalt give answer to Him in the day of Judgment. Prepare, then, thy answer for Him.

Here the speech is of righteous wealth. But unrighteous wealth, which is gathered by injustice and usury, is under a curse, as is he that gathereth it, as a transgressor of the law. He that would be saved must scatter such wealth righteously, as that which was gathered in evil, and must repent; otherwise both the wealth and his sin are retained, and the more he so gathereth wealth, the more he gathereth also sin and the wrath of God. Consider this.

sections.heading: Is this the time for such merriment?

pairs.en: 2) Is this the time for us so to make merry? (Though indeed such merriment is never befitting to Christians: *“for the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost”* [Romans 14:17].) Is this, I say, the time so to make merry? Now war, now fires, now the pestilence, now other calamities come upon us, and humble us. But men do not feel this.

How then must we humble ourselves the more? Troubles and calamities multiply, yet luxury and sins — the cause of troubles and calamities — multiply also, and the righteous God is the more provoked. What then follows from this? Greater troubles must be looked for, even as a sick man whose sickness is not healed, but is the more inflamed, must look for a greater disease; or as a fire which is not quenched, but is fanned, must the more increase. Before destruction men grow more and more mad. The Lord saith: *“except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish”* [Luke 13:3]. Dreadful is this word, for it is true: *“O Lord, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing”* [Jeremiah 10:24].

sections.heading: Our brothers fall, and we feast

pairs.en: 3) Our brothers fall by bullets, by cannon-shot and by the sword in war; others are in continual fear and sorrow — and we here make merry in folly!… We ought to have helped them against the enemy; but instead, by feasting, by drunkenness and by other sins, we sharpen the foreigner's sword against them, and so make war against ourselves!…

O bitter time and evil days! O blindness of perverse and unrepentant hearts! Is it in this sorrowful and troubled time that men should make merry? O how sin gathers strength, and godliness grows scarce!

These people do as those senseless seamen whose ship is breaking up, and yet they dance; or as those mad citizens whose city is on fire, and yet they keep festival. The fatherland groans under troubles and calamities; young men grow fewer and fewer; the treasury is exhausted by war; only the aged and the youths and the infants remain; and the matter comes home even to us; everywhere mothers, fathers, wives, brothers and friends mourn and weep for their own who have fallen in battle and who stand in danger of death — yet these revellers alone make merry, as though they were not sons of the fatherland, and with our enemies they rejoice over the troubles that surround us!…

O luxury, luxury! How thou blindest, and makest foolish, and hardenest the hearts of men! It is time to come to our senses, that we may not repent for ever, and to no purpose, with the ungodly described in the book of the Wisdom of Solomon (chapter 5).

4) How many scandals, sins and lawless deeds are found in such gatherings and merrymakings, it is impossible to number. As many words and deeds as are there, so many are the sins; as many faces, so many are the transgressors. Far from such places God and His holy Angels depart. There is the place for the devil and his evil angels, who rejoice with them that rejoice, and make merry over their ruin. Therefore their destruction sleepeth not, if they do not soon come to their senses. They have forgotten God and His righteous judgment; they *“profess that they know God; but in works they deny”* Him [Titus 1:16]. So did the rich man of the Gospel make merry; but being in torments, he crieth out and saith: *“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame”* [Luke 16:24]. So he that was bathed in wine asks for a drop of water, and receiveth it not, and shall never receive it for ever. The rich men of this day also must take heed, who make merry every day, and break the law of God, and will not so much as look upon the poor Lazaruses.

Consider these points, and so make them known to them that make merry. And if thou thyself art entangled in their nets, tear them asunder by the fear of God's Judgment, and flee from them, as Lot fled from Sodom, that with the men of Sodom thou mayest not know the trial of eternal fire.

Make them known also to others, that they who so make merry may know their sin, and may repent. And if thou dost not make them known, it shall be sin unto thee; for this is written not for thee alone, but for all.
